components.notes: S_n, centered sums S_n^(c), zero rate with positive deterministic denominators, the natural logarithm and the n >= 2 convention are defined.
Power-moment identity with infinite values, the integer-tail sandwich, both decreasing-sum bounds, the sum bound p n^{1/p} and the shift inequality are proved.
components.source_comparison: Durrett Lemma 2.2.13 (pp. 63-64): E(Y^p) = int_0^infty p y^{p-1} P(Y > y) dy by Fubini for nonnegative variables, reproduced with Tonelli and measurability.

components.notes: Statement (zero variance included; mean-mu variant), the explicit variance series with integral comparison, Theorem 2.5.6 and Kronecker; the iterated-logarithm Remark is reported and explicitly not used as a premise.
components.source_comparison: Durrett Theorem 2.5.11 (p. 87): hypotheses, a_n = n^{1/2}(log n)^{1/2+eps} for n >= 2 with a_1 > 0, the variance sum, Theorems 2.5.6 and 2.5.9; the WLOG mu = 0 remark; and the Remark that the LIL (Theorem 8.5.2) makes the rate 'not far from the best possible' are all present.

components.notes: Deletion cutoff at m^{1/p} with the boundary retained, T_n, mu_m and the contrast with the strict Feller cutoff are defined.
Statement and every proof step: change count, interval decomposition with Tonelli, integral comparison including the first interval, centered series, and the mean estimate with d_m -> 0.
components.source_comparison: Durrett Theorem 2.5.12 (pp. 87-88) with the Marcinkiewicz-Zygmund attribution and its EX^2 = infinity motivation: truncation at k^{1/p}, Borel-Cantelli, intervals [(n-1)^{1/p}, n^{1/p}], the bound (p/(2-p))(n-1)^{(p-2)/p} <= C y^{p-2}, Theorems 2.5.6/2.5.9, mu_m = -E(X; |X| > m^{1/p}) and the sum bound C n^{1/p} are all present.

components.notes: Absolute weighted summability below order one proved without independence; the signed limit follows.
Moment necessity for every p > 0 and every center, probability zero when the moment is infinite, and c = EX_1 for p >= 1 are proved.
components.source_comparison: Durrett Exercise 2.5.2 (p. 90): the converse of Theorem 2.5.12 for p > 0 is proved (with centering added).

components.notes: Both regimes (0 < p < 1 with any center; 1 <= p < 2 with c = EX_1) are proved in both directions; the p = 2 exclusion is backed by C012.
Feller normalization (a_n/n nondecreasing), Q with the inclusive tail, strict truncation Y_n and the a_0 = 0 interval convention are defined.

Both branches are written in full, including the exact count identity, the strict-truncation variance bound, a_n/n -> infinity and the mean estimate. The Section 2.5.2 framing is reported and its consequences (no nonzero almost-sure limit; Theorem 2.3.8 as the case a_n = n) are proved.
components.source_comparison: Durrett Theorem 2.5.13 (p. 89) and proof (pp. 89-90): a_{kn} >= k a_n, block comparison, max{|S_{n-1}|,|S_n|} >= |X_n|/2, identity (*), Y_n = X_n 1(|X_n| < a_n), sum_{n>=m} a_n^-2 <= C m a_m^-2, a_n/n -> infinity, the split at a_N; and p. 88 (St. Petersburg in probability versus a.s., Feller (1946), no nonzero a.s. limit, Theorem 2.3.8 special case) are all present.

components.notes: All four examples computed (fair signs; dyadic law with E sqrt X = 1+2^{1/4}+sqrt 2 and infinite mean; density (7/4)x^{-11/4} with mean 7/3 and 3/2-moment 7; dyadic tail sums). S_n/n -> infinity rests on thm:p15-extended-mean-strong-law, proved on the route before this chapter.

The order-two bound (via thm:p15-bounded-fourth-moment, independent-random-series.tex 97-114) with the tail zero-one law, the constant sequence, the critical-moment law with finite mean, and the two Feller hypothesis failures are proved.
Deterministic staircase: existence of each N_k, the summable threshold series, failure of the ratio condition and the infinite limit superior are proved.

The boundary states that the three source proofs are complete and points to existing routed results (weak laws, Feller's median necessity, St. Petersburg, weak convergence; all cited labels exist with proved= status); the LIL is reported and not used.

Partial sums, averages, the finite-limit strong-law assertion, integrable common law, pairwise independence versus i.i.d., and the moving deletion truncation Y_k, T_n with the retained boundary value are all defined.
Statement and a written head/tail epsilon proof; this is the averaging step Durrett leaves as 'it follows easily' (p. 87).

Both tail-integral identities (the second via a pointwise identity and Tonelli), the integer tail bound and the bound 2y sum_{k>y} k^-2 <= 4 on both ranges y >= 1 and 0 <= y < 1 are proved in written steps.
components.source_comparison: Durrett Lemma 2.4.4 (pp. 76-77): integral comparison for m >= 2, the y >= 1 case via [y]+1 >= 2 and y/[y] <= 2, and the 0 <= y < 1 case are all reproduced.

components.notes: Finite-change bound with an explicit R(omega), summable scaled variances <= 4E|X_1|, convergence of truncated means and of their averages, and preservation of pairwise/mutual independence are proved.
components.source_comparison: Durrett Lemma 2.4.2 (sum P(|X_k|>k) <= E|X_1|, finitely many changes, |S_n - T_n| <= R) and Lemma 2.4.3 (E Y_k^2 <= int_0^k 2y P(|X_1|>y) dy, Fubini) on p. 76, and the dominated-convergence step on p. 77, are all present.

components.notes: Geometric indices, the bound 4(1-alpha^-2)^-1 m^-2, Chebyshev, the Tonelli interchange and countably many thresholds are written out.
components.source_comparison: Durrett p. 77: k(n) = [alpha^n], [alpha^n] >= alpha^n/2, Chebyshev, interchange of the sums, geometric-series bound and 'epsilon arbitrary' are all reproduced.

components.notes: Full statement; the proof covers the nonnegative case (subsequence limit, monotone interpolation, countable alpha_l = 1+1/l) and the X^+/X^- reduction with checks of pairwise independence, identical laws and integrability.
components.source_comparison: Durrett Theorem 2.4.1 (p. 76) with the Etemadi (1981) attribution, the remark that Lemmas 2.4.2-2.4.3 are 'standard' and that the second step matters for this proof and for Section 2.5, Etemadi's X^+/X^- inspiration (p. 77), and the interpolation T_k(n)/k(n+1) <= T_m/m <= T_k(n+1)/k(n) with alpha arbitrary (pp. 77-78) are all present.

components.notes: Positive divergent nondecreasing weights, repeated weights, conditional convergence of the weighted series and the a_0 = b_0 = 0 conventions are defined.

Summation-by-parts identity, the explicit weighted-average limit with H_M, and the extension to weights that are eventually positive and nondecreasing are proved; necessity of monotonicity and divergence is shown in C013.
components.source_comparison: Durrett Theorem 2.5.9 (pp. 85-86): a_n increasing to infinity, a_0 = 0, b_m, x_m = a_m(b_m - b_{m-1}), and the average-of-b_m argument with mass concentrating on m >= M are all reproduced.

components.notes: Weighted criterion without identical laws, proved from thm:p15-variance-series-convergence (independent-random-series.tex 75-92, proved there) and pointwise Kronecker; the a_n = n specialization is proved.
Distinct random-series proof written without invoking the pairwise theorem; the role of mutual independence is stated.
components.source_comparison: Durrett Theorem 2.5.10 (pp. 86-87): Y_k, Z_k = Y_k - EY_k, the variance bound from the proof of 2.4.1, Theorem 2.5.6, Kronecker, dominated convergence and averaging are all present.

components.notes: Borel-function averages, countable families, frequencies, and the two computed averages (1/3; mean 3 with infinite second moment) are proved with the integrals computed.
Construction, pairwise independence, failure of mutual independence (1/4 versus 1/8) and the strong-law conclusion are proved.
All four boundaries (shared sign; independent nonidentical laws; dyadic infinite mean via clipped means r+1; nonmonotone and constant Kronecker weights) are fully computed.

The boundary names exactly what is proved here and what follows: Theorem 2.4.5 (proved on the route as thm:p15-extended-mean-strong-law, strong-law-applications.tex 36-48), Theorems 2.4.7 and 2.4.9, and Theorems 2.5.11-2.5.13 (next routed chapters). The added section reports the random-series rate advantage and the iterated-logarithm comparison as Durrett's assessment, not as premises.
